**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, struggling with long division, my fingers smudging the pencil lead across the page. The sentence settled in my stomach like a stone. Not because it was untrue—I *wasn’t* trying hard enough—but because it was the first time I understood that words could press down on you, could make the air thicker, could turn a simple math problem into a test of worth.

Years later, I’d learn that words could also lift. A teacher’s *"You have a way with language"* sent me floating for weeks. A friend’s *"I’m here"* held me up when nothing else could. But that first stone-word stayed with me, a reminder: language is never neutral. It builds or it erodes. It is both the architect and the wrecking ball.

---

II.

I once met a man who collected obsolete words. He carried a leather-bound notebook everywhere, its pages filled with ink in three different colors (black for nouns, red for verbs, blue for the unclassifiable). *"Sonder,"* he told me over coffee, *"is the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own."* He tapped the page. *"And ‘petrichor’—the smell of rain on dry earth. We don’t use it enough."* I asked why he did it. He said, *"Because words die when we stop saying them. And some deserve to live."*

I think about him often, especially now, in an era where language is both inflated and deflated—where we have a thousand ways to say *"I’m sad"* (depressed, blue, in a funk, vibing low) but no words left for the quiet, stubborn joy of watching sunlight hit a glass of water just right. We are drowning in language and starving for meaning.

---

III.

My grandmother used to say, *"A secret is a word you swallow."* She had a lot of them. I’d find her sometimes, sitting on the back porch at dusk, her hands folded in her lap, her mouth moving slightly, as if chewing on something too bitter to spit out. When I asked what she was doing, she’d smile and say, *"Just talking to myself, child. It’s safer that way."*

I didn’t understand then, but I do now. Some words are too heavy to give to others. They’d break under the weight. So we keep them, let them dissolve slowly in the dark of our bodies, where no one can see the shape they leave behind.

---

IV.

The internet has turned words into currency. We spend them like coins—likes, shares, retweets—each one a tiny transaction of attention. *"Viral"* used to mean something that spread like a disease. Now it’s what we hope for. We craft sentences designed to be consumed quickly, digested without thought, excreted just as fast. *"Hot take."* *"No cap."* *"Slay."* The shelf life of a word is shorter than ever. We burn through them, hungry for the next spark.

But what happens when we run out? When we’ve used up all the words, when *"amazing"* and *"terrible"* and *"love"* have been stretched so thin they mean nothing at all? Will we invent new ones, or will we just stop talking?

---

V.

I had a dream once where words were physical things. Not metaphors—*actual*. I walked into a library, and the books were alive, their spines pulsing like veins. When I pulled one from the shelf, the pages fluttered like wings. The words inside weren’t printed; they were carved into the paper, deep grooves filled with ink that shimmered when I touched it. Some words were light as feathers. Others took two hands to lift. The heaviest was *"forever."* I tried to pick it up, but it wouldn’t budge. A librarian (who may have been a raven) looked at me and said, *"Some words aren’t meant to be carried alone."*

I woke up with my fingers curled, as if still gripping the edge of a page.

---

VI.

There’s a game I play sometimes when I’m bored in meetings or waiting in line. I listen to the snippets of conversation around me and try to guess the weight of the words. *"I’ll call you later"*—light, almost weightless, the kind of thing that floats away before it lands. *"I miss you"*—heavier, but not crushing. It sits in the palm of your hand, warm. *"We need to talk"*—a boulder. A meteor. Something that leaves a crater.

The record holder so far was a woman on a park bench, speaking into her phone: *"I can’t do this anymore."* Seven words. I swear the bench sagged under them.

---

VII.

I wonder if this is why we’re so afraid of silence. Not because we have nothing to say, but because we have *too much*—because the words we *don’t* say are the heaviest of all. The unsent text. The apology swallowed. The *"I love you"* that dies on the tongue. Silence isn’t empty. It’s full. It’s a room packed with everything we lack the courage to voice.

---
VIII.

A thousand words. I’ve used most of them now. Some were easy, rolling off the fingers like pebbles down a hill. Others I had to pry out, one letter at a time, like pulling teeth. But here’s the thing about words: they’re never just yours. The moment you set them free, they belong to whoever reads them. They’ll carry different weights for different people. *"Grief"* might be a feather to one person and an anvil to another. *"Hope"* could be a lifeline or a lie.

So I’ll leave you with this: be careful with words. Not because they’re fragile (they’re not; words survive fires, wars, the slow erosion of time), but because they’re powerful. They shape worlds. They break hearts. They build bridges. They are the only magic we have left.

And magic always comes with a cost.
